title: Big-O and performance thinking
subtitle: Count the steps before you count the seconds
goal: Predict how code slows down as data grows, confirm it with timeit, and choose data structures that keep programs fast.
outcomes: Count the steps an algorithm takes and express them in Big-O
Recognise O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n²) in real code
Spot hidden loops such as in on a list, count() and pop(0)
Measure code with timeit and compare list vs set membership
Rewrite an O(n²) duplicate check as O(n)

slides.title: Mission 41: Big-O and performance thinking
slides.body:
Your code works on 100 rows. Production has **10 million**. Will it take a second, or a week?

Today you learn to predict that **before** you run anything, with Big-O: the language every developer and every interviewer uses to talk about speed.
slides.say: Welcome to phase five, Developer. Your code works on a hundred rows, but production has ten million. Will it take a second, or a week? Today you learn to predict that before you run anything, using Big O, the language every developer and every interviewer uses to talk about speed.

slides.title: Count steps, not seconds
slides.body:
Seconds depend on the device. **Steps** depend only on your algorithm.

Big-O answers one question: **when the input grows, how fast do the steps grow?** We call the input size `n`.
slides.say: Seconds depend on the device. A cheap phone and a big server give different times for the same code. Steps depend only on the algorithm. Big O answers one question: when the input grows, how fast does the number of steps grow? We call the input size n.

slides.title: Counting steps
slides.body: Two functions, same data. Count how many times the innermost line runs.
slides.expect:
n=10: one pass 10, every pair 100
n=100: one pass 100, every pair 10000
n=1000: one pass 1000, every pair 1000000
explain: One loop over the items: n steps.
A loop inside a loop: for every a, visit every b.
Try three sizes, each ten times bigger.
One pass grows 10x; every pair grows 100x.
slides.say: Let's count instead of guess. One pass touches each item once, so its steps grow in line with n. Every pair puts a loop inside a loop, so it does n times n steps. Run it and watch the gap: ten times more data makes the nested loop a hundred times slower.

slides.title: How steps grow
slides.body: Same 1,000 items, five algorithms. The gap between the last two bars is the gap between a snappy app and a frozen one.
slides.say: Here is the whole idea in one picture, for a thousand items. Constant time is one step. Log n is about ten. A single pass is a thousand. Sorting is about ten thousand. Every pair is a million. The chart switches to a log scale, because the last bar would not fit on your screen otherwise.

slides.title: The five you will meet every day
slides.body: These five cover almost all real code. Learn them with an example each.

head: Big-O
Name
Real example
rows: binary search in a sorted list
sum(items), one for loop, x in a_list

slides.say: Five classes cover almost everything you will write. Constant time, like looking up a key in a dict. Logarithmic, like binary search. Linear, like a single for loop. N log n, which is what sorting costs. And quadratic, which usually means a loop inside a loop. Learn this table by heart.

slides.title: How many steps?
slides.why: The inner loop runs 4, then 3, then 2, then 1 times: 10 in total. That's n(n+1)/2, which still grows like **n²**, so it is O(n²).
slides.say: The inner loop starts at i, so it gets shorter every time round. How many times does count go up? Predict, then run.

slides.title: Keep the biggest term
slides.body:
Big-O is about the **shape** of growth, not exact counts:
- drop constants: `3n` is **O(n)**
- keep the fastest-growing term: `n² + n + 100` is **O(n²)**
- plan for the worst case: searching a list is O(n), even if the item is sometimes first
slides.say: Big O is about the shape of growth, not exact counts. Drop the constants, so three n is just O of n. Keep only the fastest growing term, so n squared plus n is O of n squared. And plan for the worst case: when you search a list, assume the item is at the very end.

slides.title: Spot the hidden loop
slides.q: What is the Big-O of `common(a, b)` when both lists have n items?
slides.why: `x in b` looks like one step, but on a list Python checks items one by one: an O(n) loop inside your O(n) loop. Turn `b` into a set first and the whole function becomes O(n).
slides.say: This function has one visible loop. But look closely at the if line. What is its Big O when both lists have n items?

slides.title: Hidden loops in Python
slides.body: One innocent line can hide a whole loop. Know what each operation costs.
slides.say: One innocent line can hide a loop. Checking if something is in a list scans every item, but a set or dict jumps straight to it using a hash. Popping from the front of a list shifts every other item along. These costs are invisible in the code, so you have to know them.

slides.title: Halving the problem
slides.code:
n = 64
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)
slides.why: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1: six halvings. Cutting the problem in half on every step is **O(log n)**, and log₂ 64 = 6.
slides.say: Each time round the loop, n is cut in half. How many steps until it reaches one?

slides.title: Why O(log n) is a superpower
slides.body: Keep halving until one item is left. Watch how slowly the step count grows.
slides.expect:
1,000 items -> 9 steps
    1,000,000 items -> 19 steps
1,000,000,000 items -> 29 steps
explain: Each loop cuts the problem in half.
The comma in the format spec adds thousands separators.
slides.say: A billion items, and only twenty nine steps. That is why binary search, which halves the problem every time, can search a billion sorted records almost instantly. Every time the data grows a thousand times, a log n algorithm needs only about ten more steps.

slides.title: Measure with timeit
slides.body:
Big-O predicts; **`timeit`** confirms. It runs a snippet many times and returns the total seconds, so random noise averages out.

`timeit.timeit(lambda: work(), number=100)`

lines: 5000000 loops, best of 5: 45.1 nsec per loop
20 loops, best of 5: 6.12 msec per loop

slides.say: Big O predicts, and timeit confirms. It runs a small piece of code many times and gives you the total time, so random noise averages out. Developers also run it straight from the terminal. Look at these numbers: the set answers in nanoseconds, while the list needs milliseconds.

slides.title: List vs set, measured
slides.body: We divide by `number` to get the time for **one** lookup, then compare.
slides.code:
import timeit

user_ids = list(range(100_000))
user_set = set(user_ids)
target = 99_999            # worst case for a list: the very last item

list_time = timeit.timeit(lambda: target in user_ids, number=50) / 50
set_time = timeit.timeit(lambda: target in user_set, number=50_000) / 50_000

print("Both found it:", target in user_ids and target in user_set)
print("Set is faster:", set_time < list_time)
print("List is over 100x slower:", list_time > 100 * set_time)
slides.expect:
Both found it: True
Set is faster: True
List is over 100x slower: True
explain: …and the same IDs in a set.
Time 50 list lookups, then divide: seconds per lookup.
Sets are so fast we need 50,000 runs to measure them well.
The ratio is huge, so this is True on any device.
slides.say: Now let's measure it for real. We store a hundred thousand user IDs in a list and in a set, then time how long it takes to find the last one. The set uses a hash to jump straight to the answer, while the list checks every single item. Your exact times depend on your phone, but the verdict never changes.

slides.title: Your phone, your numbers
slides.body: Real timings from **your** device (µs = microseconds). Look at the pattern as `n` grows 10x.
slides.code:
import timeit

for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000]:
    items = list(range(n))
    lookup = set(items)
    t_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: n - 1 in items, number=200) / 200
    t_set = timeit.timeit(lambda: n - 1 in lookup, number=100_000) / 100_000
    print(f"n={n:>7,}: list {t_list * 1e6:9.2f} µs   set {t_set * 1e6:6.3f} µs")
slides.say: This one prints real timings from your own device, so your numbers will differ from mine. Watch the pattern, not the digits. Each time n grows ten times, the list time grows about ten times too. That is O of n. The set time barely moves. That is O of 1.

slides.title: The slow duplicate checker
slides.task:
`has_duplicates` gives the right answer, but it compares **every pair**: O(n²). On a million sign-ups it would run for hours.

Rewrite it to be **O(n)** with a set. Same behaviour: return `True` if any item appears twice, otherwise `False`.
hints: A set answers `item in seen` in O(1).
Walk the list once: if the item is already in `seen`, return True; otherwise add it.
A one-line version also works: `return len(set(items)) != len(items)`
slides.say: Here is a real performance bug. This function gives the right answer, but it compares every pair, so on a million sign ups it would run for hours. Rewrite it so it walks the list only once, remembering what it has seen in a set. The tests count your comparisons, so they will know.

slides.title: Choose the right data structure
slides.body: Most speed-ups in real projects come from picking the right container, not from clever tricks.

head: You need to…
Use
Why
rows: find a record by ID or email
add and remove at both ends

slides.say: In real projects, most speed ups come from choosing the right container, not from clever tricks. Need to ask, have I seen this before? Use a set. Need to find a record by its ID? Use a dict. Need order and positions? A list. Adding and removing at both ends? A deque. Counting? A Counter.

slides.title: Counting the O(n) way
slides.code:
from collections import Counter

votes = ["Kohli", "Rohit", "Kohli", "Bumrah", "Kohli", "Rohit"]

# O(n²): count() rescans the whole list for every name
slow = {name: votes.count(name) for name in votes}

# O(n): one pass, and Counter does the bookkeeping
fast = Counter(votes)

print(slow == dict(fast))
print(fast.most_common(2))
explain: count() is a hidden loop, run once per vote: O(n²).
Counter walks the list once: O(n).
The two most common names, with their counts.
slides.say: Here is a pattern you will spot in code reviews. Calling count inside a loop rescans the whole list for every name, which is O of n squared. A Counter does the same job in a single pass. Both give identical results, but only one survives a million votes.

slides.title: Pick the structure
slides.q: Your app checks whether a username is taken on every sign-up. There are 5 million users. What should hold the existing usernames?
options: One long string, names separated by commas
slides.why: A set answers `name in taken` in O(1), however many users you have. A list, tuple or string would scan up to 5 million entries on every single sign-up.
slides.say: Quick decision. Five million users, and every sign up must check if the username is already taken. Which container do you choose?

slides.title: Who hasn't submitted?
slides.task:
A class has roll numbers `1` to `total`. `submitted` lists who handed in homework (it can contain repeats). Write `missing(total, submitted)` that returns the roll numbers that did **not** submit, in order.

Make it **O(n)**: don't search the list once per student.
slides.starter:
def missing(total, submitted):
    # Return the sorted roll numbers from 1 to total that are not in submitted
    pass

print(missing(5, [1, 2, 4, 2]))   # [3, 5]
slides.solution:
def missing(total, submitted):
    done = set(submitted)
    return [roll for roll in range(1, total + 1) if roll not in done]

print(missing(5, [1, 2, 4, 2]))   # [3, 5]
hints: Convert `submitted` to a set once, at the top of the function.
Loop over `range(1, total + 1)` and keep the rolls that are not in the set.
Set difference works too: `sorted(set(range(1, total + 1)) - set(submitted))`
slides.say: Your turn. A class has roll numbers one to total, and a list of who submitted homework, with some repeats. Return the roll numbers that are missing, in order. Make it O of n by turning the list into a set first. The tests watch for slow searches.

slides.title: Mission 41 complete
points: Big-O describes how steps grow with the input size n, not seconds
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²): know an example of each
Drop constants, keep the biggest term, plan for the worst case
Hidden loops: in on a list, count(), index() and pop(0) are all O(n)
timeit confirms what Big-O predicts; sets and dicts make lookups O(1)
slides.say: Mission forty one complete. You can count steps, name the five common Big O classes, spot hidden loops, and prove your choices with timeit. Tomorrow we put this to work with searching, sorting and recursion, the algorithms behind every search bar and leaderboard.
